changes.motivation: When `RemainAfterExit = mkDefault true` was applied globally to all services, timer-activated services would stay in `active (exited)` state after their first run. Systemd timers use `start` semantics, so subsequent timer fires were no-ops on already-active services.
changes.summary: Modified `modules/common/systemd/default.nix` to automatically set `RemainAfterExit = mkOverride 999 false` for any service that has a corresponding timer entry. Priority 999 overrides the global `mkDefault` (priority 1000) but yields to explicit user assignments (priority 100), so timer-paired services return to `inactive` after each run while non-timer services retain the default behavior.

problems: The interaction between `RemainAfterExit=yes` and systemd timer semantics is a subtle footgun: timers call `start` (not `restart`), which is a no-op when the service is already `active (exited)`. This behavior was not documented anywhere in the codebase, so the bug was only discoverable by tracing the systemd state machine. A comment in `modules/common/systemd/default.nix` explaining why timer-paired services must not use `RemainAfterExit` would have made this self-evident.
